questions.scenario: A right-skewed feature (for example, income) violates a model's normality assumption and hurts a linear model's fit.
questions.question: Which transformation is a common first choice, and why?
options: Squaring the values, which makes the right skew worse.
Adding a constant to every value.
A log transform, because it compresses large values more than small ones, pulling in the right tail toward symmetry.
Multiplying by a constant to rescale.
questions.explanation: A log transform shrinks large values far more than small ones, so a long right tail is pulled inward and the distribution becomes more symmetric. Squaring would stretch the tail further. Adding or multiplying by a constant shifts or rescales but does not change the shape.
questions.misconception: Rescaling by addition or multiplication does not fix skew. Only a non-linear transform like log changes the distribution's shape.

questions.question: What advantage does the Yeo-Johnson transform have over the Box-Cox transform?
options: Yeo-Johnson handles zero and negative values, while Box-Cox requires strictly positive inputs.
They are identical in every case.
Box-Cox is non-parametric and Yeo-Johnson is not.
questions.explanation: Box-Cox is defined only for positive data, so it fails on zeros or negatives without shifting. Yeo-Johnson extends the same power-transform idea to the whole real line, including zero and negative values, which makes it the more general default.

questions.question: A quantity where a small fraction of items accounts for most of the total (for example, wealth or web traffic) is often modeled by which distribution?
options: The Pareto distribution, which captures heavy-tailed, power-law behavior.
questions.explanation: The Pareto distribution models power-law, heavy-tailed phenomena, the familiar pattern where a small share of causes drives most of the effect. A uniform distribution spreads mass evenly, and a normal distribution has light tails, so neither fits this shape.
